newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Violent crime rising in Buenos Aires, police say.
newsitem.headline: Violent crime rising in Buenos Aires, police say.

text.p: Violent crime is rising in traditionally safe Buenos Aires and a growing number of the criminals are foreign, Argentina's Federal Police chief said on Wednesday.

"I don't want this to be interpreted as an attack on foreigners but data shows that in 1996 15 percent of those arrested were foreigners, when 10 years ago the percentage was five," Police Chief Adrian Pelacchi told La Nacion newspaper.
He said 70 percent of Buenos Aires' estimated 8,000 squatters were foreigners "and with them come a lot who were already criminals in their own countries."
Federal police data showed there were more robberies in 1996 than 1995 but the total was still below 1993 levels, he said, but he added: "There are more armed robberies and they are more violent."

Buenos Aires, one of five short-listed candidates to host the 2004 summer Olympics, is touting itself as a "safe" option based on its reputation for relatively low levels of street crime despite its population of 12 million.

But Argentine police are going through a confidence crisis, especially the Buenos Aires Provincial Police Force, largest in the country with 48,000 officers. Some officers have been arrested for drug dealing and links with anti-Jewish bomb attacks or are suspected of involvement in the brutal murder of a newsman this year.

The governor of Buenos Aires Province, which surrounds the capital and is the country's most populous area, acknowledged on Tuesday that his police force had a serious image problem. "Every day there are more people who don't dare report a crime at a police station because they have lost their trust. When they see a patrol car at night, rather than feeling protected they feel scared," Gov. Eduardo Duhalde said.
The federal force, which polices the capital and has agents in the provinces to investigate federal crimes, is the second largest in Argentina with about 31,000 officers.
